passages.t: A second call, and a five-word sermon
passages.happening:
‘Then the word of the LORD came to Jonah a second time’ (verse 1). He is to get up, go to the great city of Nineveh, and proclaim the message God gives him (verse 2). “This time Jonah got up and went to Nineveh, in accordance with the word of the LORD. Now Nineveh was an exceedingly great city, requiring a three-day journey” (verse 3).

On the first day Jonah goes into the city and proclaims, “Forty more days and Nineveh will be overturned!” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
God gives Jonah a second chance, in almost the same words as the first. This time he goes.

Nineveh was one of the great cities of Assyria, on the Tigris. In the eighth century the royal residence was usually at Calah, with Nineveh a major royal city; Sennacherib made Nineveh the capital around 700 BC and greatly enlarged it. The three days it took to cross the city are debated. It may mean the time a prophet needed to go through the city and its districts, or the size of the wider area, or it may be part of the story's deliberate exaggeration.

Jonah's message is only five words in Hebrew, one of the shortest prophetic sermons in the Bible. It has no call to repent and no offer of mercy. The word overturned is ambiguous: it can mean destroyed, as it does of Sodom and Gomorrah, or turned around, changed. Nineveh will be overturned, but not as Jonah expects.
passages.later: The same word is used of Sodom and Gomorrah: ‘Thus He destroyed these cities and the entire plain’ (Genesis 19:25), where the Hebrew verb is overturned.
passages.asks: God gave Jonah a second chance. Ask where God has called you again after you ran the first time. And ask whether you would rather give people a warning or a way back.

passages.t: A city in sackcloth, and God relents
passages.happening:
‘And the Ninevites believed God’ (verse 5). They proclaim a fast and dress in sackcloth, from the greatest to the least. When the word reaches the king, he rises from his throne, takes off his royal robe, covers himself with sackcloth and sits in ashes (verse 6).

He issues a decree. No person or animal, herd or flock, is to eat or drink (verse 7). People and animals alike are to be covered with sackcloth, and everyone is to call out to God and turn from evil ways and ‘from the violence in his hands’ (verse 8). ‘Who knows? God may turn and relent; He may turn from His fierce anger, so that we will not perish’ (verse 9). When God sees them turn from their evil ways, ‘He relented from the disaster He had threatened to bring upon them’ (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Fasting and sackcloth were widespread signs of mourning and repentance. Sackcloth was coarse cloth of goat hair worn next to the skin, and sitting in ashes showed humiliation and grief. The king's actions reverse every sign of royal dignity, one by one. Including animals in public mourning sounds strange, but there is evidence from the ancient world of animals in mourning rites; the Greek historian Herodotus describes Persians shaving their horses in mourning. It shows how completely the city humbled itself, and it prepares for the book's last line, where God mentions Nineveh's cattle.

The title king of Nineveh is unusual, since Assyrian rulers were called king of Assyria. Some take it as the storyteller's focus on the city, others as a sign that the book is not interested in historical detail, others as a local ruler or governor. No Assyrian record describes a citywide repentance, and scholars weigh that silence differently. Some who read the book as history point to unrest in Assyria in the first half of the eighth century, including plague, revolts and the eclipse of 763 BC. Others note that such links cannot be proven.

The key word is turn. The people turn from their evil, and God turns from the evil, the disaster, he had threatened. Who knows is hope without presumption: the Ninevites have no promise, only a warning.
passages.later: Joel uses the same words, ‘Who knows? He may turn and relent’ (Joel 2:14), and David said ‘Who knows?’ as he prayed for his dying child (2 Samuel 12:22). Jesus said, ‘The men of Nineveh will stand at the judgment with this generation and condemn it; for they repented at the preaching of Jonah’ (Matthew 12:41).
passages.hard:
Was Jonah's prophecy false, since Nineveh was not destroyed in forty days?

Jonah announced a judgment that sounded unconditional, and it did not happen. Most interpreters answer that prophecies of judgment in Scripture often carry an unstated condition. Jeremiah says that if a nation God has warned turns from its evil, he will relent (Jeremiah 18:7-10). The Ninevites themselves seem to have understood this, hoping that God might turn. On this view the prophecy did what it was meant to do: it brought repentance, and God's relenting fulfilled his purpose. Some also note that Nineveh was destroyed in the end, in 612 BC, as Nahum announced, after its later violence.

The chapter's concern is not whether Jonah's reputation as a prophet survives. It is whether God's mercy is right, the question Jonah himself raises next.
passages.asks: The most feared city of the age turned, from the king down. Ask whether there is anyone you have decided is beyond turning. And the king said, Who knows? Ask what it would mean for you to turn to God with no claim but hope.
